summary.text: A 46-year-old man with hypertension and no prior thyroid disease was incidentally found on routine laboratory evaluation in July 2024 to have elevated TSH (6.5 mIU/L) with elevated free T4 and free T3; TSH had been normal (3.4 mIU/L) earlier, with free T4 not assessed. He denied hyperthyroid symptoms apart from headaches attributed to poorly controlled hypertension.

After referral to Endocrinology in October 2024, vital signs, physical and thyroid examination, and visual fields were normal with no stigmata of acromegaly, and there was no family history of thyroid or pituitary disease. Repeat thyroid function tests in October 2024 showed persistent central hyperthyroidism. The work-up also found an elevated alpha subunit and normal IGF-1, prolactin, testosterone and cortisol, and excluded resistance to thyroid hormone and assay interference.

Pituitary MRI showed a 17 × 14 × 15 mm sellar mass centered on the right pituitary gland with upward displacement of the optic chiasm and right prechiasmatic optic nerve, small cystic areas and broad contact with the right cavernous internal carotid artery.

He underwent an uncomplicated endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal resection in December 2024; pathology showed a thyrotroph-type pituitary neuroendocrine tumor (up to 70% TSH-positive cells, 50% growth hormone staining). About six weeks postoperatively thyroid function had normalized (TSH 2.1 mIU/L, free T4 1.30 ng/dL, total T3 132 ng/dL) with normal IGF-1, prolactin, testosterone and cortisol.
